questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
I chose my destination primarily because I speak some Italian and wanted to improve my language skills. Also I have spent longer periods of time in Italy before and wanted to go back and try to live there properly and experience every-day life there. 
Furthermore the University of Milan had a virology course that I really wanted to follow, which I unfortunately was not able to follow in the end.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had an amazing time, and I think it was an incredible and important experience to have. I enjoyed living abroad, trying something different from what I am used to, adapting to situations that turn out different than what you expect - and of course meeting so many amazing people and exploring a wonderful culture along the way.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Not always super easy, but when you emailed them with questions they replied very fast and was always very helpful.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had a lot of email correspondance with different people about which couses I could follow etc. It was confusing to figure out, but they are very helpful and in the end it all worked out. They are all very available with help and answers, both in the administration and the professors.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I would have liked more comprehensive information with more time before the arrival, instead of having to wait until the last minute. And it would have been nice to have more information automatically instead of having to ask for it.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Fairly easy. Personally I found an apartment on AirBnB that was available for long term rent, and shared it with another student.
But there are several firms renting out to students for a couple of months at a time.
Be careful in the facebook groups, a lot of scamming going on there.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is more expensive than on-campus housing, but I appreciate having my own space and not sharing rooms with another person.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
They recommended that I followed the courses in a master, but there was some of them I didn't want and i would be 3 ECTS short, so I told them that i wanted to pick my own courses. I was allowed to do this, but many of the courses I wanted had a lot of overlapping hours so I ended up with some different courses than what I had hoped for. They were still very interesting though.
The process of registration was also a bit confusing, but they were very helpful when answering questions.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
When you log in to your university page, there is a module where you can fill out the courses you would like to register for. Then later you get a confirmation if you ask for it.
You chance your course registrations several weeks after the semester has started so you can try out different things, or change your mind if you need to.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a guide document on how to register, and also the erasmus coordinator was available through email.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Some of the classes I wanted had a lot of overlapping hours, so I was restricted in choosing certain things, but ultimately I ended up with courses I had had preapproved from home and nothing I didn't find interesting.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Find more courses than what you are required to take, because some of them might not be possible to follow. And if they recommend you to do something, just be insistant that you don't want to do that, and they will probably allow you to do it your way.
Also, some courses are taught in italian but has english course material and will allow you to do the exam in english if you ask the professor.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took MA level courses to have courses taught in english instead of italian. Even though I was a BA student it was easy enough to follow the material, it was not very complicated but in some cases the curriculum was quite large.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I only had lectures, no seminars or class activities (apart from some laboratory work), and no reading material either.
I mainly learn by doing, so it was very difficult for me to have no assignments or focused teaching.
The material was very interesting but I missed the more involved teaching style of Copenhagen University.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Communicable and non-communicable diseases (8 ECTS)
Pathogenetic basis of disease (12 ECTS)
Applied Pharmacology to biotechnology (7 ECTS)
Italian language course (3 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I particularly enjoyed communicable and non-communicable diseases. The communicable part had very interesting topics and competent professors.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: My personal spending was quite high, but that was something that was pretty purposeful, I was there to have a good time. And this also includes a ski trip and several trips around the country.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transportation and supermarkets are very cheap, also alcohol. Restaurants were quite expensive compared to other expenses, and rent was generally very steep.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a volunteer driven organisation called ESN Erasmus Student Network that organizze several activities every week, especially in the beginning. This includes city tours, italian language cafe, picnic in the park, karaoke night, volleyball, outdoor fitness, wine dinners etc. There are so many things, and I recomend going to it all - it is a great way to meet new friends and explore the city. And a great way to get reccomendations from the volunteers who are all working or studying in Milan themselves.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Ski trip! It's called Erasmus Snow Week, it is super cheap and so much fun. Lots of international and italian students for the opening of the season. We went to the Dolomites for 4 days of skiing and it was so great. 
Also all the ESN events, so much fun and a great way to connect with people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Milan is exceptionally well connected to the rest of the country, so I reccomend going on trips as much as you can to different cities. There are trains to basically everywhere, all of the time.
We went to the Como lake, Bergamo, Venice, Cinque Terre in Liguria, Rome and Sicily (Palermo) among others for extended weekend trips, or day trips. So easy and relatively cheap and easy, and can be planned spontaneously.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Certain things can be frustrating with the ways they do things there, but it always works out in the end - so it is a good lesson to learn, and quite in the italian spirit: just relax, everything will work out fine in the end, don't be too bothered, and take it one step at a time.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to the ESN events and get to know the volunteers, or ask your italian classmates for help to start up the conversation. Or live in a dorm or a shared apartment with local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There can be a bit of a language barrier sometimes, but they always do their best to understand you, and if you do the same it will be fine. And also, the university is a lot less structured than what I was used to which can be frustrating, but again, write them an email and it will all work out just fine.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I think Italian people are generally very open and hospitable, and eager to help if you ask. Also they have wonderful food, and a beautiful country. I had an absolute pleasure staying there for a longer time, and if you have a little hedonist hidden inside you, this is the place for you.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Don't worry if you can't find the info or haven't heard anything. Just write them an email.
2. Go see the country! Hop on a train and you can get basically anywhere in no time.
3. Go on the ski trip! Also if you are no good at skiing. Will be worth it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Speaking Italian is definitely not necessary, but learning a few words and phrases can be useful in certain situations - and they are very eager to teach you something if you ask as well!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting lots of wonderful friends from all over Europe, and learning to adapt to unexpected situations.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All the paperwork and emails and registrations and such takes a toll on you but are all worth it. When you are finally there you can just enjoy it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
